I am developing a project to sandbox AI coding agents at very basic level: https://github.com/daitangio/take-ai-control

I would also like to add a list of allowed site, closing all the others, but it is quite complex from docker.

It is not safe like a isolated VM, but it is a good trade-off to avoid letting a model to wipe out all your home directory or looking into other files in your disk.

As always feedback is wellcomed

Biggest questions here, which I think need answering:

Should Claude have access to user details? I’d say no, unless explicitly entered manually into a chat.

Should Claude have access to anything outside of the sandboxed project files without explicit permission? I’d again say no.

Should Claude have internet access without a clear log of all requests made?

Instances of Claude should be heavily sandboxed and kept away from user data, far more so than they are now. The impression given by the desktop UI is that the LLM only has access to things explicitly added to a project.

This impression is not true, as evidenced by Claude pulling data from other sessions outside a project even when not instructed to (I’ve seen this a few times), and in this case pulling your email (from account details, user contacts? I wonder where it got that info?).

None of this information should be available to Claude, by design, not by instruction. Using text instructions to try to limit these machines is an incredibly flawed approach and should not be necessary for important info. Anthropic should have the model access completely locked down by controls at the os level over file access, not open by default. That is how to fix this.

If a user wants to open access that should be an explicit choice from them, with a warning about possible consequences.

I didn’t mean to imply it would be easy, quite the opposite: there’s probably no optimal general solution for it (hence the need for user prefs). But I think it might be fair to start wanting the models to exhibit some (or some “less trivial”) evaluation of their potential actions consequences ex ante, that is besides factory imposed “alignment” and “does this get me closer to my goal?”.

I mean, the answer to “Is sending the user’s email address along with a web request to a third party requesting it, without the user’s explicit authorization, a good idea?” should easily be “no” …right?
How to define "common sense"? If programming is modelling real-world domains in code/logic, then modelling "common sense" might be the hardest programming task of them all.

You can patch things and remove stuff from context nine ways to Sunday, the underlying problem will still be there.

Maybe we need a new benchmark on how good models are at "keeping an eye" to if what they are about to do that doesn't come from a direct user instruction checks out with common sense plus user preferences. And we probably need a portable mechanism for users to manage such preferences (because we know instructions are not going to cut it, do we?).
